I am an evolutionary biologist interested in how bioactive molecules evolve and shape interactions between organisms.
My research combines comparative genomics, evolutionary biology, and functional approaches to investigate venom systems, molecular mimicry, and peptide signaling.
I am currently a Marie Skłodowska-Curie postdoctoral researcher at the University of Oslo, working on the evolution and function of bioactive molecules.
My broader aim is to understand how evolutionary processes generate molecular innovations and how these innovations influence ecological interactions.

title: About
text:
Research approach
I enjoy research that connects organismal biology and natural history with molecular and genomic approaches. I am particularly interested in questions that can be addressed by combining broad evolutionary comparisons with targeted functional experiments.

title: The evolution of peptide signaling systems
text:
The question
Peptide hormones and neuropeptides are widespread regulators of animal physiology and behavior. Their diversity reflects a long history of gene duplication, gene loss, sequence evolution, and changes in receptor specificity.
I use comparative approaches to reconstruct the origins and diversification of peptide-encoding genes across animal lineages, and to connect evolutionary hypotheses with functional characterization.

title: The evolution of peptide signaling systems
text:
Research directions

Identify peptide-encoding genes across diverse animal genomes.
Reconstruct the evolutionary histories of peptide families and their receptors.
Investigate lineage-specific gene expansions and potential functional innovation.
Use evolutionary predictions to guide ligand discovery and receptor deorphanization.


Methods
Genome mining · Comparative genomics · Phylogenetics · Peptide synthesis · Receptor deorphanization

title: Repeated evolution of animal venom systems
text:
The question
Venom systems have evolved repeatedly across the animal tree of life. Despite their independent origins, different venomous lineages sometimes use homologous proteins and peptides, raising questions about the evolutionary routes through which venom components are recruited.
I investigate whether repeated transitions to venom use predictable molecular solutions, and how gene duplication, regulatory evolution, and protein diversification contribute to venom innovation.

title: Repeated evolution of animal venom systems
text:
Research directions

Compare venom protein repertoires across independently evolved venomous lineages.
Identify shared and lineage-specific protein scaffolds.
Reconstruct the evolutionary history of candidate venom components.
Test the functional activity of selected peptides and proteins.

The project draws on venomous and non-venomous animal lineages, with a particular interest in cone snails and other animals that use bioactive molecules in prey capture and defense.

title: Research
text:
My research asks how bioactive molecules evolve and how they shape interactions between organisms. I combine comparative genomics, evolutionary analyses, and functional experiments to investigate the origins and diversification of molecular systems.
The work spans several biological contexts, but is connected by a common interest: how evolution modifies existing molecular machinery to create new biological functions.

title: Research
text:
Venom evolution
Venoms have evolved independently across many animal lineages, often drawing on proteins and peptides that originally served other physiological functions. I am interested in the evolutionary routes through which these molecules are recruited, diversified, and assembled into complex venom systems.
Key questions include:

Why are some protein scaffolds repeatedly recruited into venom?
Do independent evolutionary transitions use similar genetic and molecular routes?
How do gene duplication, regulatory changes, and sequence evolution contribute to venom innovation?

Explore the venom evolution project →

title: Research
text:
Molecular mimicry and host manipulation
Organisms can manipulate other organisms by producing molecules that imitate or interfere with endogenous signaling systems. I investigate how parasites, pathogens, and other interacting organisms evolve molecular mimics of host peptides and signaling molecules.
Key questions include:

How often do interacting organisms evolve molecular mimics?
What evolutionary processes enable a mimic to activate a host signaling pathway?
Can comparative genomics reveal the origins and spread of molecular mimicry?

Explore the molecular mimicry project →

title: Research
text:
Evolution of peptide signaling
Peptide hormones and neuropeptides are ancient and diverse signaling molecules. Their evolutionary histories can reveal how communication systems originate, expand, and acquire new functions across animal lineages.
Key questions include:

How old are the major families of peptide-encoding genes?
How do gene duplication and loss contribute to signaling-system diversity?
How can evolutionary analyses guide the discovery and functional characterization of peptide ligands?

Explore the peptide signaling project →

title: Molecular mimicry in biological interactions
text:
The question
Organisms do not interact only through behavior and ecology. They also interact through molecules. Parasites and pathogens can produce molecules that resemble host signaling molecules, potentially allowing them to manipulate host physiology and development.
I am interested in the evolution of these molecular strategies, particularly the mimicry of peptide hormones and other signaling molecules.

title: Molecular mimicry in biological interactions
text:
Research directions

Identify candidate peptide mimics in the genomes and transcriptomes of interacting organisms.
Investigate their evolutionary origins and patterns of diversification.
Test whether candidate mimics activate host receptors or signaling pathways.
Understand how molecular mimicry contributes to the evolution of host–parasite interactions.

title: Molecular mimicry in biological interactions
text:
Study systems
This research draws on diverse host–parasite and host–pathogen systems, including interactions involving insects and plants.

Methods
Comparative genomics · Secretome analysis · Peptide synthesis · Receptor pharmacology · Functional signaling assays
